nativeRendering.summary: Browsers paint form controls using the OS theme. Custom CSS overrides that, changing how the box is rendered.
nativeRendering.title: How Browsers Handle Native Elements
nativeRendering.p1: Browsers draw certain initial elements, mostly form elements, using a native rendering mode driven by your operating system's UI engine rather than standard CSS layout rules. The OS paints the button onto the screen, which is why a native button without any custom styling looks slightly different on Windows, macOS, iOS, or Android.
nativeRendering.p2: At first paint, the default styles you see in the browser's stylesheet aren't traditional CSS rules; they are system rules. They essentially tell the browser to ask the operating system what its current theme looks like and copy it.
nativeRendering.p3: The moment you apply a custom border, padding, or background, this link to the operating system breaks. The browser terminates the native rendering mode and hands full layout control over to its own CSS painting engine.
nativeRendering.p4: This switch is why a "2px" border you set manually might look thicker than the "2px" border the browser was just drawing: it is the exact same number, but rendered by a completely different paint engine.
nativeRendering.p5: This shift from native to custom rendering creates a critical accessibility responsibility. Overriding native styles often strips away the browser's default, highly optimised behaviours.
nativeRendering.p6: When you style a button with CSS, you must manually code explicit design features that native buttons usually handle for you:
nativeRendering.focusRingsBody: You must ensure clear keyboard focus indicators exist, maintaining at least a 3:1 contrast ratio so keyboard users don't lose their place.
nativeRendering.hitAreasBody: The button must maintain a sufficient physical size (at least 44x44 pixels) for touch screens and users with limited motor control.
nativeRendering.contrastBody: Text-to-background contrast must remain high enough to prevent the button from becoming unreadable for users with low vision or colour blindness.

remUnits.summary: rem is a CSS length unit that scales with the user's browser font-size preference. Using it for layout values respects accessibility settings that px values ignore.
remUnits.title: How REM units work
remUnits.intro: rem stands for "root em". It's a CSS length unit whose value depends on the root font-size of the page, which is the font-size set on the html element. By default, browsers set this to 16px, so 1rem typically equals 16px. The root font-size can change, and rem-based values change with it.
remUnits.responsiveP1: A user can change their browser's default font-size in browser settings, often labelled "page font size" or "default font size". When they do, the root font-size of every web page they visit changes. CSS values written in rem scale automatically. CSS values written in px do not.
remUnits.responsiveP2: Set a button to width: 5rem. At the default root size of 16px, the button is 80px wide. If the user sets their browser root to 20px, the button becomes 100px. A button set to width: 80px stays at 80px no matter what the user prefers.
remUnits.a11yP1: WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text requires that text can be resized up to 200% without loss of content or functionality. If you use px for both your text and the container around it, increasing text size can cause overflow, clipping, or broken layouts. Using rem for the container as well means the layout scales with the text.
remUnits.a11yLead: For users who need larger text:
remUnits.a11yPoint1: A user with low vision may set their default browser font size to 24px or more.
remUnits.a11yPoint2: A user with a cognitive impairment may prefer larger, clearer text to reduce reading effort.
remUnits.a11yPoint3: An older user may find smaller text physically uncomfortable to read at length.
remUnits.a11yOutro: In all of these cases, a rem-based design respects the user's preference. A px-based design ignores it entirely.
remUnits.comparisonLead: Three common length units, three different behaviours:
remUnits.comparisonPx: px is absolute. 16px is 16px, always. It ignores the user's preferences.
remUnits.comparisonEm: em is relative to the element's own font-size, which inherits from its parent. This makes em values unpredictable in deeply nested layouts.
remUnits.comparisonRem: rem is relative to the root font-size only. Consistent across the page, and responsive to user preferences.
remUnits.whenRemLead: Most CSS values that relate to layout and typography are good candidates for rem:
remUnits.whenRem1: Font sizes, especially headings and body text.
remUnits.whenRem3: Widths and heights of components that contain text.
remUnits.whenRem4: Border-radii on elements that hold text.
remUnits.whenPx1: Hairline borders that you want pixel-precise regardless of user settings.
remUnits.whenPx2: Specific visual details that shouldn't scale, like dividers or small icons.
remUnits.whenPx3: One-off values from design tools when you need to match a mockup exactly.
remUnits.whenOutro: A useful test: if changing the value would affect how the user reads or interacts with the page, rem is probably the right choice. If it's purely decorative or structural, px is fine.

vagueLabel.summary: Automated tools verify a button has a name, but they can't tell whether the name is meaningful out of context.
vagueLabel.title: Why button labels matter
vagueLabel.intro: Automated tools check that a button has an accessible name, but they can't check whether that name is meaningful. A button labelled "OK" or "Submit" passes the automated check just as cleanly as "Save changes to invoice". Real users are left to guess what it does.
vagueLabel.matterP1: Screen reader users often navigate by element list, a feature that reads out every button, link, or heading on the page in sequence. Out of that context, a bare "OK" or "More" tells them nothing about what the button actually does. The user has to either guess or backtrack into the surrounding content to find out.
vagueLabel.matterP2: Sighted users are affected too. Clear labels reduce cognitive load. A well-named button answers "what will happen if I press this?" before the user has to read the surrounding context. It's especially valuable for users with attention or memory impairments, anyone in a hurry, or non-native speakers parsing an unfamiliar UI.
vagueLabel.goodLead: Two patterns produce labels that read clearly out of context:
vagueLabel.goodVerbNoun: Verb + noun. "Save changes" beats "Save". "Delete account" beats "Delete". The noun tells the user what the action operates on.
vagueLabel.goodResult: Describe the result, not the mechanism. "Send email" beats "Submit". It tells the user what will happen, not which technical pattern triggers it.
vagueLabel.okLead: Single-word or generic labels are not always wrong. They can be appropriate when:
vagueLabel.okContext: The surrounding visual context already provides meaning. A search input with a button labelled "Search", or even just "Go", is unambiguous in that setting.
vagueLabel.okPattern: The button is part of a familiar pattern, like the "Submit" of a contact form or the "Next" of a wizard step. Users recognise these conventions without further explanation.
vagueLabel.okIcon: A visible icon disambiguates the action. A printer icon next to the word "Print" is redundant; the icon alone may suffice (with an appropriate aria-label).
vagueLabel.testP: A practical check: read the label out loud, alone, with no visible context. If a colleague can guess what the button does, the label is doing its job. If they can't, expand it until they can.

formWrapping.summary: Wrapping a button in a form reveals submit and reset behaviour, and exposes the accidental implicit-submit risk of an unconfigured button.
formWrapping.title: Why wrapping a button in a form matters
formWrapping.intro: AccessLab lets you toggle a form wrapper around any button you are auditing. Several button variants only exhibit their real behaviour inside a form, and a plain {buttonText} without an explicit type attribute can result in unintuitive results when inside a form.
formWrapping.defaultsTitle: What buttons do by default inside a form
formWrapping.defaultsLead: Each button variant has a specific default behaviour when activated inside a form:
formWrapping.defaultsSubmit: Submit-typed buttons (button with type="submit", and input with type="submit") submit the form. The browser gathers the form's values, fires the submit event, and dispatches the request described by the form's action and method attributes.
formWrapping.defaultsReset: Reset-typed buttons restore every form control to its initial value. They do not submit anything.
formWrapping.defaultsButton: Button-typed buttons (type="button") do nothing on their own. They stay inactive until JavaScript adds a click handler. This is the recommended variant for any interactive control that is not a form submission.
formWrapping.defaultsOutro: Outside a form, all four variants behave identically: they fire the click event and nothing else. The form wrapper is what surfaces the differences.
formWrapping.resetScopeP1: Reset only affects form controls the user can edit: text fields, textareas, selects, checkboxes, radios, file inputs. Buttons themselves are not affected. A button's value and name attributes are part of the markup, not user state, so there is nothing to roll back.
formWrapping.resetScopeP2: This is why a form containing only a reset button has nothing to reset. The reset event still fires, but no visible change occurs. Once you add an editable input to the form, clicking reset restores that input to its initial value while leaving the button untouched.
formWrapping.pitfallTitle: A common pitfall: accidental form submission
formWrapping.pitfallP1: A button element with no type attribute defaults to type="submit" according to the HTML specification. Outside a form this has no effect. Inside a form it is one of the most common causes of accidental form submissions.
formWrapping.pitfallP2: Here is how the problem typically appears. A developer adds a button inside a form to expand an extra field, attaches a click handler, and releases the code. Every time the user clicks the toggle, the form submits. The bug is easy to miss in code review because the markup looks correct.
formWrapping.pitfallP3: The fix is always the same: write the type attribute explicitly. Use type="button" for any control that should not submit, and type="submit" for the one that should. This makes the intent clear at a glance, wherever the button appears in the code.
formWrapping.whenTitle: When to use a form wrapper
formWrapping.whenLead: Wrap interactive controls in a form when:
formWrapping.whenSubmit: The control represents a transaction. A login screen, a comment box, a search field, a sign-up flow. The browser's built-in form-submission semantics are doing real work for you.
formWrapping.whenValidation: You want to use built-in HTML validation. The required attribute, type="email" pattern checking, and the constraint validation API only run on submit when controls are inside a form.
formWrapping.whenAutofill: You want the browser to autofill. Browsers detect form fields by their association with a form element and decide whether to offer saved credentials, addresses, and payment methods.
formWrapping.whenMultiSubmit: You need more than one submit button in the same form. The button value attribute lets the server tell which button was clicked. See the related topic for the full pattern.
formWrapping.whenNotLead: Do not wrap in a form when:
formWrapping.whenNotInteractive: The button triggers a UI action, such as opening a modal, expanding a section, or toggling a state.These are not transactions. Use type="button" without a surrounding form.
formWrapping.whenNotLink: The action navigates to a different page or scrolls to an anchor. Use a real anchor element with href instead.
formWrapping.preventionP1: If a form must exist for accessibility or semantic reasons but you want to handle submission entirely in JavaScript, attach event.preventDefault() in the submit handler. The form fires the submit event, your handler intercepts it, and the browser navigation is cancelled.
formWrapping.preventionP2: AccessLab's preview iframe takes exactly this approach. The shell attaches a single submit listener to the preview area and calls preventDefault on every form submission, so clicking a submit-typed button inside the iframe never causes the iframe to navigate away to a blank page. The toast confirming the click still fires because the click event is independent of the form's submission.
formWrapping.relatedButtonValue: How the value attribute behaves on a button

buttonDisabledStates.summary: The disabled attribute makes a button inert: no clicks, no focus, no submit. The aria-disabled alternative keeps the button reachable while announcing its unavailable state.
buttonDisabledStates.title: Disabled states on buttons
buttonDisabledStates.intro: Buttons can be marked as unavailable in two different ways, and the choice between them changes how the button behaves for every user. Knowing the difference prevents a common class of accessibility bugs where a button looks disabled but does not behave that way.
buttonDisabledStates.whatLead: Setting the disabled attribute on a button or input button changes four things at once:
buttonDisabledStates.what1: Click events are not fired. The browser blocks them at the event-dispatch layer, so JavaScript handlers never run.
buttonDisabledStates.what2: The button is removed from the keyboard focus order by default. Tab and Shift+Tab skip past it.
buttonDisabledStates.what3: The button does not participate in form submission. A disabled submit button cannot trigger the form, and its value is not included in the form's payload.
buttonDisabledStates.what4: The form's implicit-submit-on-Enter behaviour skips disabled buttons when picking which submit control to fire.
buttonDisabledStates.whatOutro: The result is a control that is visually present but completely inert. For genuinely unreachable functionality, this is the right tool.
buttonDisabledStates.screenReaderTitle: How screen readers announce disabled buttons
buttonDisabledStates.screenReaderP1: Screen readers announce a disabled button differently from an enabled one. NVDA and JAWS say "dimmed" or "unavailable". VoiceOver says "dimmed". The element is still in the accessibility tree, so a user navigating the page sequentially will hear it, but they will be told they cannot interact with it.
buttonDisabledStates.screenReaderP2: Some virtual-cursor modes skip disabled controls entirely. Users may not realise the button exists or what it does. This is the accessibility cost of disabling: the user gets less information than a sighted user who can read context around the dim button.
buttonDisabledStates.ariaDisabledP1: Setting aria-disabled="true" on a button takes a different approach. The button remains in the focus order, remains clickable, and continues to fire events. Screen readers still announce it as disabled, but the button is reachable, and your JavaScript can decide what to do when it is activated.
buttonDisabledStates.ariaDisabledP2: A common pattern: a form's primary submit button gets aria-disabled while validation is incomplete. When the user clicks it anyway, the page scrolls to the first invalid field and explains what is wrong. The user receives feedback instead of silence.
buttonDisabledStates.ariaDisabledP3: The visual styling comes from a CSS selector like [aria-disabled="true"]. The HTML disabled attribute has its own browser-supplied dim styling; aria-disabled does not, so you must style it yourself.
buttonDisabledStates.ariaDisabledP4: Choose between the two based on what the user should be able to do. If the button is genuinely unreachable, use disabled. If you want users to be able to click it and get feedback explaining the disabled state, use aria-disabled and handle the click in JavaScript.
buttonDisabledStates.whenAvoidTitle: When to avoid disabled buttons altogether
buttonDisabledStates.whenAvoidP1: Some accessibility practitioners argue that disabled buttons should be avoided in favour of always-enabled buttons with clear, visible error messages. The argument is that a disabled submit button gives the user less information than an enabled button that explains exactly what is wrong.
buttonDisabledStates.whenAvoidP2: There is no WCAG rule against the disabled attribute. Both approaches can be accessible. The aria-disabled pattern is a middle ground: the button looks unavailable, the user can still click it, and the click handler provides specific feedback.
buttonDisabledStates.guidance1: Use disabled when the button is genuinely inert. A deleted record cannot be re-deleted; that button should be disabled and unreachable.
buttonDisabledStates.guidance2: Use aria-disabled when you want the user to be able to click and receive feedback. Validation-pending submit buttons are the canonical example.
buttonDisabledStates.guidance3: Never communicate disabled state with colour alone. The browser's dim styling is one cue; pair it with the disabled attribute or aria-disabled so the meaning is conveyed to assistive technology as well.
buttonDisabledStates.guidance4: Consider whether disabled is the right pattern at all. An enabled button with a clear error message often serves users better, particularly users who cannot easily perceive the dim styling.
buttonDisabledStates.relatedAccessibleName: What counts as an accessible name

buttonTypes.summary: The type attribute on a button element controls what the button does inside a form. Omitting it leads to one of the most common bugs in web forms.
buttonTypes.title: Why button type matters
buttonTypes.intro: Every button element has a type attribute. It controls what the button does when activated inside a form. There are three valid values. The choice between them is small in code and large in consequence.
buttonTypes.typesLead: A button element accepts three values for the type attribute:
buttonTypes.typeSubmit: type=submit. The button submits the parent form when clicked. The form gathers its values, fires the submit event, and dispatches the request described by the form's action and method attributes. This is the default if the type attribute is missing.
buttonTypes.typeReset: type=reset. The button restores every form control to its initial value. It does not submit anything. Rarely used in modern interfaces because users often click it by accident.
buttonTypes.typeButton: type=button. The button does nothing on its own. It stays inactive until JavaScript adds a click handler. This is the right choice for any interactive control that is not a form submission.
buttonTypes.whyExplicitP1: A button element with no type attribute defaults to type=submit, according to the HTML specification. Outside a form this has no effect. Inside a form it is one of the most common causes of accidental form submissions.
buttonTypes.whyExplicitP2: The pattern is easy to miss in code review. A developer adds a button inside a form to expand an extra field, attaches a click handler, and releases the code. Every time the user clicks the toggle, the form submits. The markup looks correct because the developer never thought to set the type explicitly.
buttonTypes.whyExplicitP3: Setting the type attribute explicitly makes the intent visible at the place the button is written. type=button for any control that should not submit, type=submit for the one that should. The compiler does not check this. Code review does not always catch it. Writing the attribute by hand on every button is the most reliable defence.
buttonTypes.keyboardP1: Buttons must be operable from the keyboard. The browser handles this for native button and input elements automatically, but the exact keys differ between the two, and users (along with their assistive technology) rely on the expected behaviour.
buttonTypes.keyboardP2: A button element activates on both Space and Enter. The browser fires a click event whichever key the user presses. This dual binding is what screen reader users and keyboard-only users expect.
buttonTypes.keyboardP3: Input buttons activate on Space when focused. Inside a form, pressing Enter on any other input also triggers the form's primary submit button, even if focus is not on the button itself. This implicit-submit-on-Enter behaviour is what lets users submit a search form without reaching for the mouse.
buttonTypes.keyboardP4: Custom buttons built from div or span elements break this entirely. They are not keyboard-operable by default. Adding role="button" does not restore Space and Enter handling automatically; you must wire up your own keydown listeners and stop the page from scrolling on Space. Always start from a real button element and style it, rather than starting from a styled div and bolting on accessibility.
buttonTypes.guidanceLead: A few rules of thumb that prevent most type-attribute confusion:
buttonTypes.guidance1: Always set the type attribute on every button element. Treat the implicit default as a hidden risk.
buttonTypes.guidance2: Use type=button for any button that triggers JavaScript-only behaviour: opening a dialog, expanding a section, toggling a state, anything that is not a form submission.
buttonTypes.guidance3: Use type=submit for the single primary action of a form. If a form needs more than one submit button, see the related topic on the value attribute for the multi-submit pattern.
buttonTypes.guidance4: Avoid type=reset unless you have specific evidence that users want it. The cost of an accidental click is high and the value of a form-clearing button is low.
buttonTypes.relatedFormWrapping: Why wrapping a button in a form matters
buttonTypes.relatedButtonValue: How the value attribute behaves on a button

buttonValueAttribute.summary: On a button element, the value attribute is hidden form data, not a label. Screen readers ignore it entirely. This is the opposite of how value works on an input button.
buttonValueAttribute.title: How the value attribute behaves on a button
buttonValueAttribute.intro: The value attribute is a frequent source of confusion because it does completely different things depending on which element it is set on. Understanding the split prevents a class of subtle accessibility bugs.
buttonValueAttribute.differenceTitle: The difference between button and input elements
buttonValueAttribute.differenceP1: On an input element with type=button, type=submit, or type=reset, the value attribute is the visible text shown to the user. It is also the accessible name announced by assistive technology. Set value=Save and the input button reads Save on screen and to a screen reader.
buttonValueAttribute.differenceVoid: The reason input behaves this way is that {inputElement} is a void element. HTML defines it as self-closing with no children, so writing {invalidMarkup} is invalid and browsers silently correct it. With nowhere inside the element for text content, the specification puts the visible label on the value attribute. Same attribute, two roles by necessity: the visible label and the form data the server receives.
buttonValueAttribute.differenceP2: On a button element, the value attribute does not appear on screen at all. It is hidden form data, included with the form submission when the user clicks the button. The visible text is whatever you put between the opening and closing tags of the button.
buttonValueAttribute.differenceP3: Two elements that look identical in the UI carry the value attribute in completely different roles. A developer used to one pattern may carry the assumption over to the other and create a button that appears to have a label but does not.
buttonValueAttribute.useCaseTitle: When you would actually use the button value attribute
buttonValueAttribute.useCaseP1: The most common reason to set a value on a button is when a single form has more than one submit button, and the server needs to know which one was clicked.
buttonValueAttribute.useCaseP2: Imagine a form for writing a blog post. At the bottom you have two submit buttons. One is labelled Save as Draft and carries value=draft. The other is labelled Publish Now and carries value=publish. Both buttons share the same name attribute, for example name=action. When the user clicks Save as Draft, the form submits and the server receives action=draft in the request data. When they click Publish Now, the server receives action=publish.
buttonValueAttribute.useCaseP3: The server reads the name and value pair to decide what to do next. Without the value attribute, the server would have no way to distinguish which button submitted the form.
buttonValueAttribute.a11yTitle: Why the value attribute is invisible to screen readers
buttonValueAttribute.a11yP1: When a screen reader announces a button, it reads only the accessible name. For a button element, the accessible name comes from the text content between the opening and closing tags, or from an aria-label if one is set. The value attribute is not part of the accessible name computation at all.
buttonValueAttribute.a11yP2: This creates a quiet accessibility failure. A developer writes a button with the visible text X and sets value=Delete Item, expecting the value to convey the action. A screen reader user hears only X, button. They have no idea that this button is intended to delete something.
buttonValueAttribute.a11yP3: The fix is to make the action part of the visible label, or to add an aria-label that describes the action in plain words. For example, aria-label=Delete Item paired with the X icon. The screen reader now announces Delete Item, button, regardless of what value is set for the form data.
buttonValueAttribute.mismatchTitle: The link to label in name
buttonValueAttribute.mismatchP1: The same example reveals another concern. WCAG Success Criterion 2.5.3, Label in Name, requires the accessible name of a control to contain its visible text. Voice control users speak the visible label to activate a control.
buttonValueAttribute.mismatchP2: An X button with value=Delete Item and no aria-label has visible text X. A voice user saying click Delete Item finds nothing matching, because no control on the page is named Delete Item. Saying click X works, but only because the user can see the visible text.
buttonValueAttribute.mismatchP3: If the developer adds aria-label=Delete Item to fix the screen reader problem, a new issue appears. The visible label is X but the accessible name is Delete Item. The two no longer agree. Axe flags this with the label-content-name-mismatch rule.
buttonValueAttribute.mismatchP4: Resolving both at once means pairing a visible label with a matching accessible name. Either replace the X with the word Delete and let the visible text speak for itself, or pair the X icon with aria-label=Delete Item and accept that voice users will need to speak the action rather than the icon. The choice depends on which user groups the product prioritises and whether the icon is reinforced elsewhere.
buttonValueAttribute.guidanceLead: A few rules of thumb that prevent most value-attribute confusion:
buttonValueAttribute.guidance1: Treat value on a button element as form data only. If you want a label, set the text content of the button, not the value attribute.
buttonValueAttribute.guidance2: Treat value on an input button as both the label and the form data. The same string fills both roles. Make sure the string is meaningful in both contexts.
buttonValueAttribute.guidance3: When building multi-submit forms, give each button visible text that matches its intent. Save as Draft and Publish Now are clearer than reusing a single Submit button with hidden value differences.
buttonValueAttribute.guidance4: When an icon must stand in for text, add an aria-label that describes the action. Do not rely on the value attribute to convey meaning to assistive technology.
buttonValueAttribute.relatedFormWrapping: Why wrapping a button in a form matters

accessibleName.summary: The accessible name is the label assistive technology announces for an element. Browsers compute it from several sources in a specific order, and some sources that look like labels do not count.
accessibleName.title: What counts as an accessible name
accessibleName.intro: Every interactive element on a page needs an accessible name. It is the string that a screen reader announces, that voice control software listens for, and that automated tools check when verifying a button or input is labelled. Without one, the element is effectively anonymous to users who cannot see it.
accessibleName.whyP1: A screen reader user navigating by element list hears only the accessible name of each control. If a button has no name, it is announced as just "button", with no information about what it does. The user must either guess or move focus to it and listen for surrounding context, which is slow and unreliable.
accessibleName.whyP2: Some voice-control users navigate by speaking the text they see on the screen. If the hidden 'accessible name' in your code doesn't match that visible text, the software won't recognise their voice command and nothing will happen.
accessibleName.precedenceTitle: How the browser picks the name
accessibleName.precedenceLead: Browsers compute the accessible name by checking sources in a defined order, taking the first one that yields a non-empty value:
accessibleName.precedence1: aria-labelledby. If set, the browser collects the text content of the referenced elements and uses that. This wins over everything else.
accessibleName.precedence2: aria-label. If set and aria-labelledby is not used, the aria label attribute's value becomes the accessible name.
accessibleName.precedence3: For form fields, an associated label element. Either a label with a for attribute pointing at the input's id, or a label that wraps the input directly.
accessibleName.precedence4: For buttons and links, the text content inside the element. Whatever you put between the opening and closing tags.
accessibleName.precedence5: The title attribute. A fallback that browsers and assistive tech treat inconsistently. Avoid relying on it.
accessibleName.countsLead: These provide a reliable, well-supported accessible name across browsers and assistive technology:
accessibleName.countsAria: aria-label and aria-labelledby. The most explicit way to set the name. Use aria-label when the label is a fixed string, aria-labelledby when the label already exists as visible text elsewhere on the page.
accessibleName.countsContent: Visible text content inside a button or link. The most natural option for buttons that already have a text label.
accessibleName.countsAssoc: An associated label element on a form field. The for/id association or a wrapping label element is the standard way to label inputs and is understood everywhere.
accessibleName.countsAlt: The alt attribute on images and on input type=image. This is how the accessible name is provided for image-based controls.
accessibleName.doesntCountLead: These look like labels to a sighted user but are not part of the accessible name computation:
accessibleName.doesntPlaceholder: The placeholder attribute on an input. Some assistive tech reads it as a fallback when nothing else is set, but it disappears the moment the user types, and the support is inconsistent. Never rely on it as the only label.
accessibleName.doesntNearby: Visible text near the element. A heading above a button, a paragraph beside an input, a column header next to a checkbox. The browser has no way to know that text describes the control unless the relationship is declared with aria-labelledby or a label element.
accessibleName.doesntStyling: Visual styling alone. An icon, a colour, a position on the page. The element looks meaningful to a sighted user but provides nothing to anyone using a screen reader.
accessibleName.doesntColor: Colour or shape. Using red text to mean "required" or a downward chevron to mean "expand" only works for sighted users. Pair the visual cue with text that is part of the accessible name.
accessibleName.doesntButtonValue: The value attribute on a button element. Screen readers announce only the text content of the button. The value is hidden form data sent to the server, not a label.
accessibleName.mismatchP1: When a button has both a visible text label and an aria-label, the two should match, or the aria-label should at least contain the visible text. WCAG Success Criterion 2.5.3 (Label in Name, Level A) requires it. Axe has a rule called label-content-name-mismatch that flags violations.
accessibleName.mismatchP2: The classic example: a button shows "Save changes" but has aria-label="Save". A sighted user reads "Save changes" and tells their voice control software to "click Save changes". The software searches the accessible names of every control on the page, finds only "Save", and nothing matches. The button is unreachable by voice.
accessibleName.mismatchP3: The fix is straightforward. Either remove the redundant aria-label and let the visible text speak for itself, or make sure the aria-label contains every word that appears visibly on the button. Adding extra context is fine: aria-label="Save changes to invoice" works because "Save changes" is still inside it.
accessibleName.guidanceLead: A few rules of thumb that prevent most accessible-name problems:
accessibleName.guidance1: Prefer visible text content over aria-label. The visible text is the accessible name automatically. There is nothing to keep in sync and no chance of mismatch.
accessibleName.guidance2: Use aria-label when the control has no visible text. The classic case is an icon-only button. Describe the action in plain words: "Search", "Close dialog", "Open menu".
accessibleName.guidance3: When you do use aria-label alongside visible text, include the visible text inside it. "Save changes" plus aria-label="Save changes for invoice 4521" is fine. "Save changes" plus aria-label="Save" is not.
accessibleName.guidance4: Test by reading the accessible name out of context. If a colleague hearing only the announced name can guess what the button does, the label is doing its job.
accessibleName.relatedButtonValue: How the value attribute behaves on a button

invisibleText.summary: When text colour matches its background exactly, automated contrast checks are skipped. But the text disappears.
invisibleText.title: "Invisible" Text Slips Past Automated Tests
invisibleText.intro: When text colour matches its background colour exactly, the text completely disappears from view. However, the code is still there. A screen reader will still read the words out loud, search engines will still index them, and the browser still builds space for them. But a sighted user will never see them.
invisibleText.skipTitle: Why Automated Checkers Deliberately Skip This
invisibleText.skipP1: Most automated accessibility tools skip contrast tests when the text colour and background colour are an exact match. They do this to avoid giving "false alarm" errors.
invisibleText.skipP2: Using matching colours is a common, though outdated, trick developers use to intentionally hide content from sighted users while keeping it available for screen readers (like hidden form labels or extra context for links). Because an automated tool cannot tell the difference between a mistake and an intentional design choice, it simply skips the test.
invisibleText.skipP3: The moment you change one of the colours by even a tiny fraction, the tool can calculate the contrast ratio again and will flag it as an error. Testing platforms built for human exploration fill this gap because they assume a person is checking the colours on purpose, meaning the chance of it being a deliberate hiding trick is almost zero.
invisibleText.productionP1: Accidentally invisible text is one of the easiest bugs to miss before launching a website. A developer's design file might look perfect, but a conflicting line of code or a broken variable in production can cause the colours to overlap, leaving text completely invisible while still passing every automated test.
invisibleText.productionLead: This creates a split user experience:
invisibleText.productionSplitScreenReader: Screen-reader users will hear the text perfectly and assume the page is fine.
invisibleText.productionSplitSighted: Sighted users will see an empty space or an unlabeled button, assuming the page is broken.
invisibleText.productionOutro: Catching this requires manually inspecting the final, computed colours on the screen, which standard quality assurance checks often miss.
invisibleText.wcagLead: Official web accessibility guidelines require text to stand out clearly from its background:
invisibleText.wcagAA: Level AA (Standard): Requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text.
invisibleText.wcagAAA: Level AAA (Highest): Raises that requirement to 7:1.
invisibleText.wcagOutro: A 1:1 ratio (where the text and background are identical) is a total failure of both standards.
invisibleText.fixTitle: How to Fix It, or Hide Text Safely
invisibleText.fixMistakeLead: If the invisible text is a mistake:
invisibleText.fixMistakeBody: Update your code to use distinct text and background colours that meet the required contrast ratios.
invisibleText.fixIntentLead: If you actually want to hide the text for screen-reader users only:
invisibleText.fixIntentBody: Do not use colour-matching. Instead, use a proper modern hiding technique. This usually involves a CSS class that shrinks the element out of sight (using properties like {pos} and {clip}) without removing it from the page's code. This safer method ensures the text remains accessible even if a user overrides your colours, turns on high-contrast mode, or highlights the text.
